items.title: Australian Regulator Finds More Suspected Audit Misconduct at Big Four Firms

items.summary: Bank Indonesia's governor Destry Damayanti told a parliamentary hearing on Nov 25 that the central bank assumes its benchmark interest rate will remain at 6% throughout 2027, unchanged from its year-end-2026 expectation. The figure appears in BI's budget proposal to Parliament for next year.
items.title: Indonesia central bank expects to keep benchmark rate at 6% in 2027, governor says

items.summary: Researchers from The University of Hong Kong and ByteDance Seed have open-sourced Laminar, an asynchronous reinforcement learning post-training framework for large language models and long-horizon agents. According to the launch blog, the core design goal is to stop forcing every rollout trajectory and GPU to wait on the slowest one—a bottleneck that consumes most of the GPU time in teams training coding agents with long, skewed rollouts.
items.title: ByteDance and University of Hong Kong Researchers Open-Source Laminar, an Asynchronous RL Post-Training Framework

items.summary: In a letter responding to Daniel Fung's article 'Science Talk: Are we medicalising childhood?' (Nov 23), reader Foo Siang Yian shares an observation from her daily work in the food and beverage industry, noting that she almost every day sees young children sitting at dining tables with tablets or smartphones placed directly in front of them. Rather than interacting with their family members during meals, many appear occupied with screens throughout the meal, leading her to wonder whether society is becoming too dependent on digital devices to keep children occupied while overlooking the importance of everyday human interaction. She argues that family mealtimes should offer more than just eating, providing valuable opportunities for parents and children to communicate, share experiences, ask questions, listen to one another, and develop meaningful relationships—opportunities essential for helping children build emotional resilience and social skills. Foo Siang Yian suggests a simple solution: putting away devices and making time for conversations at the table. She echoes Fung's conclusion that resilient children are built not by expanding clinical services but by strengthening 'the places they call home.'
items.title: Reader Urges Families to Put Away Screens at Mealtimes

items.summary: A coalition of 39 state attorneys general and the District of Columbia's attorney general filed a Nov. 20, 2026 objection in federal bankruptcy court seeking to exclude sensitive data and models trained on it from Character.AI's divestiture, arguing that questions about how those assets were built must be resolved before sale. The company is proceeding under Judge Brendan Shannon, with an auction for its AI models, training datasets, and users' private conversations scheduled for Dec. 1. In their filing, the states asked the court to exclude specific categories of sensitive data and the models trained on them, citing similar cases in which the Federal Trade Commission ordered companies to destroy models developed using improperly obtained information — including WW International and Kurbo (2022), Everalbum, and European Data Protection Board guidance identifying model deletion as a possible remedy for unlawful use of personal data. The states' filings assert that Character.AI told its proposed buyer it kept records identifying where transferred training data came from and which consents applied, urging those records be reviewed thoroughly.
items.title: State Attorneys General Seek to Pause Character.AI's December Bankruptcy Sale Over Kids' Data

items.summary:
Meta employees have expressed concern over the company's push to replace human moderators with artificial intelligence, claiming the technology is leading to mistakes with potential sweeping political consequences. The social media company, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has been experimenting with AI-driven moderation for years, first introducing it in 2017 to filter out violent extremist content. This March, Meta announced it was 'transforming our approach' by rolling out 'more advanced AI systems' to moderate content across its apps, framing the change as a way to improve enforcement.

Several Meta employees said that behind the scenes this push to AI was accompanied by mass layoffs across the company, severely affecting staff responsible for reviewing content on its platforms. One described Meta's content moderation as now operating with 'skeleton teams', some cut by at times half or two-thirds of their staff. 'It's been really a mess,' they said, adding that on several recent occasions they had gone to discuss an issue with a specific content moderation team, only to find that entire team was now gone.

Meta has long sought inexpensive ways to moderate the vast volumes of content posted each day to its platforms. It has faced legal action from former outsourced content moderators in Kenya, who described struggling with PTSD and severe mental health issues after being paid as little as $1.50 (£1.13) an hour to view and evaluate extremely graphic content that users attempted to post.

Meta employees say AI systems that the company is now using struggle with nuance, especially in languages other than English, and frequently remove content that should not be taken down. 'You are trying to gut all human reviewers, which are kind of essential for making these nuanced decisions and policy decisions,' said one employee. 'Of course there are going to be mistakes that are going to happen.' The employee said that because algorithms were automated, and worked at greater speed than humans, these mistakes could happen at a greater scale. The employee said Meta was removing lower-paid contractors, such as those in Kenya, and the full-time employees who would handle more complex content moderation.

Once a post is taken down, there is far less recourse for the affected accounts than before. 'Even if you know someone at Meta, it's still very difficult to get through to someone who is actually going to be able to help you, especially if it's a highly nuanced case,' the employee said. 'It's so much more difficult now.'

The growth in AI moderation comes as researchers monitoring online censorship have noticed a new phenomenon: sudden restrictions on Instagram and Facebook accounts, often during pivotal political moments. Some of these have been isolated occurrences, such as Meta's suspension of the US No Kings account in the run-up to the US midterm elections. Others have amounted to 'mass takedowns', unfolding over the course of days and hitting dozens of social media accounts.

It is a growing phenomenon, the consequences of which could 'shape the political future of entire nations', said Martha Dimitratou, the founder of the group Repro Uncensored, which monitors digital censorship. Repro Uncensored has tracked these takedowns in Brazil, the EU, Turkey and the US. The Guardian reported on a wave of account takedowns on Meta platforms late last year, affecting accounts posting queer content and those dedicated to reproductive health across Europe. Accounts backing the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, were restricted or suspended from Instagram in the feverish days of Brazil's election runoff, according to Repro Uncensored. Meta said most of the Brazilian takedowns were to comply with valid court orders or electoral regulations.

The numbers of affected accounts appear to be rising: Repro Uncensored documented 210 incidents of account takedowns on Meta in 2025, and 657 in the first six months of 2026. Meta employees who spoke to the Guardian said AI moderation had a role in such incidents as algorithms worked faster, and with less nuance, than human reviewers. 'The effect of it is you see these sweeping takedowns,' one said.

But they also said they could not rule out political considerations in how Meta's algorithm was designed. Meta's systems are opaque, even to its employees. They are a combination of LLMs – large language models, like chatbots – and older algorithms that filter content. There are 'thousands of levers and factors that weigh into how things are ranked', said one employee, and these change constantly.

The employees suggested that at times Meta's use of AI had allowed the company to obscure more controversial decisions it makes in how it moderates political content. They gave the example of how Meta made adjustments to its algorithm in late 2023 that drastically limited the number of posts that appeared from people in Palestine.

The company rejected allegations of bias and said it had previously carried out independent human rights due diligence in relation to the conflict, and since 2022 had been working to implement the resultant recommendations, including by 'introducing a system that detects and prioritises content to moderators most likely to understand that particular Arabic dialect'.

One employee said AI offered 'plausible deniability'. It afforded 'exactly the kind of ambiguity that they hide behind', they said.

In response to questions from the Guardian, a Meta spokesperson said: 'Everyone on our platforms is subject to the same set of rules, and any claims of enforcement based on political affiliation or advocacy are baseless. While we have long used AI to help enforce our community standards, earlier this year we began experimenting with more advanced AI systems that can more quickly and accurately catch violations with fewer mistakes. The latest tests show that on average these systems make 13% fewer mistakes than humans when enforcing against violating content, while finding 10% more actual violations – and we give people opportunity to appeal decisions if they think we've got it wrong.'
items.title: Meta Insiders Concerned Over Push to Replace Human Moderators with AI

items.summary: A cartoon from First Dog on the Moon poses the question of what real or imagined horrors are waking people up at 4am, framing it as a captioned item. The piece notes that we are in the most globally anxious period since World War II, though this characterization is attributed to the author's own words with the caveat 'I made this up but it sounds true.' The text also includes promotional content directing readers to sign up for email notifications when First Dog cartoons are published and to visit the First Dog shop for merchandise and prints.
items.title: First Dog on the Moon Cartoon Addresses Global Anxiety

items.summary: Unknown attackers reportedly breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the US Central Intelligence Agency, according to a source familiar with the matter who spoke to The New York Times. The cyberattack was carried out using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing framework and also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. While the CIA and ODNI have not yet responded to a request for more details, no classified data or systems were exposed in the breach; the source stated that 'the hack did not involve our classified networks or classified information, and no other systems are currently at risk.' Hours after the report, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed it was investigating a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. After detecting the attack, FinCEN took some systems offline as a precaution and directed banks to use the Financial Institutions Hotline to file reports because some services may be unavailable. BleepingComputer reached out to a FinCEN spokesperson with questions about the incident but did not receive an immediate response.
items.title: Hackers Breach CIA OSINT System Using ARTEX AI Framework

items.summary: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a $20 million financing package to develop Kyrgyzstan's first utility-scale floating solar project. The funding supports construction of a 15 MW plant at the Chakan Hydropower Plant 5 near Bishkek, built on an existing reservoir and connected to the grid, which is projected to generate around 20 GWh annually once operational. A 100 kW pilot array has already been constructed on the same reservoir.
items.title: ADB Approves $20 Million Financing for Kyrgyzstan's First Utility-Scale Floating Solar Plant

items.summary: A research team from the Netherlands' Delft University of Technology (TU Delft) investigated the outdoor soiling behavior of ethylene tetrafluoroethylene (ETFE) frontsheets over one year, finding they suffered 1% to 2% higher soiling losses than glass. ETFE is a lightweight, transparent fluoropolymer used as a protective frontsheet in flexible solar modules.
items.title: TU Delft research finds ETFE solar frontsheets suffer higher soiling losses than glass

items.summary: Malaysia's state energy company Petronas has forecast that the global liquefied natural gas market will remain relatively tight in 2027, with elevated prices likely to persist until additional supply becomes available. Executive VP and chief executive for gas and maritime business Datuk Adif Zulkifli stated this expectation as quoted by Bernama, attributing continued pressure on LNG markets to ongoing Middle East supply disruptions. The forecast depends on several factors including the duration of conflict in the region and the pace of global LNG supply growth, which has accelerated because importers are seeking alternatives to Qatari and Emirati gas. Qatar has struggled to restore LNG flows while oil exporters have boosted exports through ship-to-ship transfers; although such transfers were reported earlier outside the Strait of Hormuz, they appear less widely adopted by LNG exporters than by oil producers. U.S. LNG exports reached all-time highs this year with a similar trend expected into 2027, and Africa is emerging as another major source, with sub-Saharan African exports projected to rise 175% by 2034 following development of new projects in Mozambique, Nigeria, Senegal, and Mauritania. Separately, Rystad Energy cited El Niño conditions that may bring warmer weather and a milder-than-normal winter across key Northern Hemisphere LNG-consuming regions as factors that could weaken short-term gas demand growth by curbing heating needs and easing price pressure, while persistently high prices might encourage greater reliance on coal-fired power generation in Asia. The report was authored by Irina Slav for Oilprice.com.
items.title: Petronas Forecasts Tight Global LNG Market Through 2027

items.summary: The Solar & Storage Show 2026 – Ludhiana is scheduled for the one-day event on Tuesday, 26 November 2026 at Regenta Central Klassik in Ludhiana, Punjab. Organised by FirstVIEW, the gathering will bring together policymakers, utility representatives, developers, manufacturers and industrial energy buyers to discuss expanding solar adoption and how storage can help meet demand for reliable power.
items.title: Punjab's Solar & Storage Show 2026 to be held in Ludhiana on November 26, 2026

items.summary: Goldman Sachs has forecast that the proliferation of data centers will drive demand for natural gas in the United States over the next two years, estimating that some 52 GW of new data center capacity could be added to the grid in 2028 alone. In a note cited by Reuters this week, the bank's analysts wrote that year-to-date, data-center power capacity and demand have increased by nearly 30% in the US, contributing to more than one third of total U.S. power demand growth. The analysts said they expect growth acceleration in data centers to be driven not only by a higher volume of facilities but also by increasingly larger physical footprints and higher power density.
items.title: Goldman Sachs Forecasts U.S. Natural Gas Demand Surge from Data Center Boom

items.summary: On November 25, Amazon announced it will launch its Amazon Autos service in the UK in early 2027, marking its first expansion of the online car-buying marketplace beyond the United States. Hyundai was named as one of the first partners to offer new and used electric, hybrid, and petrol models at launch, including the IONIQ 3, IONIQ 5, KONA, and i20. Used cars from dealer group Vertu Motors will also be listed when the service goes live in the UK. Amazon said that more brands and dealers would be announced in the coming months.
items.title: Amazon to launch Amazon Autos in the UK in early 2027

items.summary:
Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX have advanced discussions on a potential merger valued at roughly $3.2 trillion, which would make it the largest corporate deal in history if completed—though no final agreement has been reached as of this reporting.

According to a Financial Times report dated November 24, both companies engaged five directors and three investment banks to negotiate terms. On SpaceX's side are Ruelof Botha and Randy Glenn; on Tesla's side are Robin Denhom, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, and Jack Hartung. The FT noted that all these directors have prior business relationships with Musk but were considered financially independent by the relevant committees.

The combined valuation is estimated at approximately $3.2 trillion (about 3,200 billion dollars), based on SpaceX's estimated valuation of roughly $1.7 trillion and Tesla's market value of about $1.5 trillion. Such a figure could place the new company among the world's five most valuable companies.

The FT report claims an announcement may occur in December. Both companies are considering an all-stock deal rather than cash payment; Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs advise SpaceX, while Evercore prepares financial models for Tesla. Musk had said in October that independent special committees were formed to avoid conflicts of interest, with him keeping himself out of the negotiations.

JPMorgan indicated that a merger could ease SpaceX's path into the S&P 500 index, estimating passive fund purchases could reach about 10% of free-float shares. However, SpaceX would still need to meet listing period and profitability requirements to join independently. The article emphasizes that talks are ongoing and no official confirmation exists for either a completed deal or a December announcement.
items.title: Tesla-SpaceX $3.2 Trillion Merger Talks: Directors and Banks Engaged

visual.alt: Bar chart. SpaceX estimated valuation 1.7; Tesla market value 1.5; Combined merger valuation 3.2.

items.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer accused reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Tuesday of shipping 'extremely advanced chips to China' and violating U.S. export control laws, calling the move 'the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the space race.' Schumer characterized it as an 'unfathomable failure of enforcement by the Trump administration,' while fellow Democrat Chris Van Hollen called Huang's reinstatement 'exhibit A' of political corruption in the administration's big tech and AI policy. Nvidia's board had reinstated Huang on Monday after President Donald Trump intervened, telling company leadership he assured them that Huang did not pose a national security risk despite questions about his relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated tech executive accused of acting as a Chinese asset and routing advanced chips to Beijing through her datacenter company Megaspeed. Van Hollen said he intends to scrutinize Huang's efforts 'to increase and accelerate the export of high-end chips to China' when the CEO appears before the Senate banking committee on December 3, joining several other appearances next week with skeptical lawmakers from both parties as well as transcribed interviews with the House foreign affairs committee, select committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and House intelligence committee. Van Hollen cited a series of ties between Huang and Trumpworld as evidence of executive influence over administration policy, including Nvidia's $25m donation to Trump's White House ballroom project, Huang's personal holdings of Nvidia stock, his contribution to Trump's inauguration fund, and attendance at a $1m-a-plate dinner at Mar-a-Lago. President Trump defended his involvement in the reinstatement on Monday via CNBC interview, arguing it would be 'a bigger threat' for Nvidia to lose Huang's 'brain power,' while confirming he had provided the board with assurances regarding national security concerns: 'I spoke to them... And I convinced them.' Congressional reaction was broad and bipartisan. Democrat Gregory Meeks called the decision 'yet another example' of how 'the wealthy and well connected are held to a different standard,' while GOP Senator John Curtis said Huang was 'right to step down' when his extramarital affair came to light, questioning what changed just 11 days after Nvidia announced his departure. Matt Pearl, a CSIS director specializing in national security, geopolitics, and technology, noted unanswered questions about Huang's conduct remain because no investigation has occurred—such probes normally take 'at least a year'—with the board instead relying on representations from senior U.S. government officials including Trump himself, effectively outsourcing the investigation; Pearl warned this could weaken how national security concerns are raised inside government and make it difficult for intelligence community members or Secretary Marco Rubio to give honest assessments of risks involving prominent individuals like Huang. Senator Elizabeth Warren argued the administration 'needs to explain to Congress what input was given and by which senior officials' to support reinstatement, while emphasizing that Huang's return increases urgency in passing bipartisan export control bills into law so Nvidia does not lobby against them. Incoming House oversight chair Robert Garcia said Trump's actions must be investigated further because no president who has invested in a private company should influence its board decisions. Republican Senator Tom Cotton warned of China obtaining advanced chips through smuggling and remote access, calling the Megaspeed controversy 'just the tip of the iceberg,' unresolved while Huang holds his job back; he pledged to pass bipartisan chip export-control bills including his Chip Security Act one way or another. Pearl also flagged succession planning for senior executives forced to step aside as a concern, noting that reinstating Huang makes it difficult to act on such issues again since firing and rehiring repeatedly looks foolish. Some Republicans directed scrutiny toward the White House equally: Senator John Kennedy said he was 'less interested in talking to Mr Huang,' whose affair he dismissed as 'the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,' but more interested in testifying Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over allegations that his department slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Earlier this month, Bessent said he had pushed for months to sanction Megaspeed—which would prevent the firm from purchasing Nvidia chips—while appearing to blame Lutnick's department for the delay: 'Commerce has the pen.' The U.S. will add Megaspeed to its trade blacklist after Commerce implemented a rule last week banning remote access to advanced AI chips and servers through data centers in third countries. Van Hollen, who is backing Senate rules reform allowing expedited consideration of bipartisan AI legislation and supporting penalties for technology companies that develop agents endangering the public, said it would be 'a good sign' if some Republican senators expressed alarm over Huang's reinstatement given recent years when they buried their heads in the sand.
items.title: Schumer Accuses Nvidia's Jensen Huang of Violating US Export Controls After Reinstatement

items.summary:
Regulator Ofgem announced that UK energy bills will rise by about 26%, with typical monthly costs increasing by roughly £37 during the first three months of January, according to a report published Monday. The increase is attributed primarily to higher wholesale gas prices driven by the Iran war; suppliers' paid wholesale gas prices rose 33% over the previous three months. For households in England, Scotland and Wales paying by direct debit using typical energy amounts, annual bills would climb from £1,723 to £2,166 if sustained for a year.

The government plans to pay millions of households £100 per month starting 4 January to help cover winter costs, on top of an existing electricity VAT cut. Additionally, the warm home discount will reduce bills by £150 for six million households receiving benefits this winter. Ofgem's director general for markets, Neil Kenward, stated that conflict in the Middle East continues driving energy costs higher and said suppliers have been written to about their responsibilities toward customers during the cold period.

The price cap sets a maximum per unit of energy rather than total bills; electricity average unit prices will rise from 26.32p to 32.69p per kilowatt-hour on January 1, while gas increases from 7.97p to 10.96p per kilowatt-hour—higher than during the Ukraine invasion period. Daily standing charges are set at 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.

Charities and suppliers expect debt levels to rise, with Citizens Advice chief executive Dame Clare Moriarty warning of a "brutal winter" and forecasting a wave of emergency support requests. Energy UK described the government funding as poorly targeted and insufficient against growing customer debt. The increase is noted as the largest since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove prices up significantly.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said families would be "deeply concerned" by another bill rise, while Labour shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie criticized the government over green levies and an EU scheme he says risks pushing bills higher. Individual household costs vary; for every £100 currently spent on energy, the new cost will be about £126.
items.title: UK Energy Bills to Rise by 26% from January

items.summary: The Trump administration is set to unveil a new batch of tariffs despite midterm exit polling that found most voters viewed them negatively. According to Semafor, the plans were reported by a person familiar with them; NBC News exit polls showed 8 in 10 voters believe President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the economy. Senate Majority Leader John Thune signaled to Semafor that more Republicans may join Democrats in pushing back on the president's trade agenda. However, Trump is not deviating: Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is expected to roll out results of an investigation into market-distorting production levels—so-called excess capacity—in dozens of countries, including China, as soon as Tuesday. The probe began prior to the election and has also raised concerns among Democrats. The resulting Section 301 tariffs will vary by country and are not expected to surpass levels set by trade deals.
items.title: Trump Administration Plans New Tariffs Despite Negative Midterm Exit Polls

items.summary: The UK energy regulator Ofgem announced that typical annual dual-fuel bills will rise by 26% in January to £2,166 for households paying via direct debit, up from £1,723 — the sharpest increase in years and a third consecutive quarterly rise. The cap applies between 1 January and 31 March and affects roughly 20 million households on standard variable tariffs; about 10 million on fixed tariffs will not be affected while their deals remain in place. Ofgem's director general for markets, Neil Kenward, attributed the increase to ongoing conflict in the Middle East pushing up international gas prices, noting that rising gas costs outpace electricity price increases as generation shifts toward renewables.
items.title: Britain's Energy Price Cap Jumps to £2,166 as Middle East Conflict Drives Costs Higher

items.summary: Singaporean billionaire Sea founder and CEO Forrest Li said he was advised against accepting the presidency of the Football Association of Singapore but felt compelled to take the role, which he assumed in April 2025. Speaking at the Singapore University of Social Sciences' JY Pillay Distinguished Speakers Series on Wednesday (Nov 25), Mr Li cited his chairmanship of Lion City Sailors from 2020 and a desire to restore national pride for a country that supported him early in life as informing his decision, arguing football could provide the shared memory and unity now missing among younger generations who see Singapore as already perfect. He recounted behind-the-scenes challenges since taking office, including converting Bishan Stadium into an AFC-compliant venue within three weeks when the National Stadium was booked for a Lady Gaga concert; he said the Sailors' Asian Football Confederation Champions League Two final was hosted there on May 18 and won despite Singapore losing. Mr Li drew parallels to his leadership of Sea, which owns e-commerce platform Shopee, online games developer Garena, and digital financial services provider Monee, describing how 'crazy moves only look good in hindsight' after success came from taking 'unintuitive and risky' decisions such as moving into e-commerce from gaming, launching Shopee mobile-first, and expanding it into Brazil. On content-driven marketing or 'shoppertainment,' he said Shopee was embracing short-video discovery expected to coexist with search-based shopping while differentiating through logistics rather than low prices alone. He recalled receiving an Economic Development Board grant for his startup in 2010 as a foreigner, described it as 'unbelievable,' and urged Singapore to remain open-minded on immigration so the small country stays connected globally, adding that its size is also an advantage when people band together with unity, echoing founding leaders' mindset. He closed by wishing Singaporeans would make staying hungry and foolish part of their enduring culture.
items.title: Sea's Forrest Li Defends 'Crazy' Move to Lead Singapore Football Association

items.summary: The author argues against the idea that avoiding disempowerment requires protectionism, using an example of twenty important math problems where allowing AIs (with human guidance) solves seventeen while humans solve one and two remain unsolved versus banning or limiting AIs so only three are solved over a longer period. The author contends that although the latter scenario involves more agency as unaided humans achieve greater things, the former produces more discovery, possibly more usefulness, and far greater marginal impact of total human effort including building the AIs. Questioning which scenario represents greater disempowerment, the author suggests it is not well defined but appears to them that humans are more disempowered in the latter case where only three problems get solved. The author then poses hypothetical scenarios about taking credit for an unpublished Chinese economics manuscript or declining a targeted EV grant to do work oneself rather than feeling empowered by protectionism or DEI for humans, describing such approaches as phony triumphs because someone else could have done it better. Reflecting on being an academic economist competing against the entire world and noting de facto open borders in the U.S. academic job market since university employers get visas for hires even today, the author concludes they are not persuaded by empowering humans through protectionism and DEI for humans, believing instead that humans will be empowered best by finding their true marginally most important contributions and making those whether or not it involves doing exactly the same things as today.
items.title: Author Rejects Protectionism as a Path to Human Empowerment Amid AI Debates

items.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo reimposed a ban on cobalt exports effective next week in an effort to raise the price of the metal, for which it holds the world's largest reserves. The restriction sent shares of some Chinese miners soaring, highlighting their dominance over global cobalt production and its role as a key ingredient in the energy transition. According to Kinshasa, the move is part of plans to build strategic reserves of several key minerals to strengthen control over supply amid competition between China and the US for access to Africa's mineral resources; while Washington seeks to loosen Beijing's grip on these chains, Chinese firms continue to dominate many critical-mineral supply networks.
items.title: DRC Reimposes Cobalt Export Ban as Prices Fall

items.summary:
Domestic energy prices are set to rise in January under Ofgem's new price cap, affecting millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales. The BBC spoke with three people about how they're reducing their gas and electricity costs.

Kelly Anne Harvey, a 44-year-old building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool with a combined household income of £60,000, currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus. She's seeking a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise after her family fell into arrears previously. To manage costs she pays by direct debit—typically £138 cheaper annually than paying when bills arrive—and uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators so central heating runs less often. Her household participates in Octopus's energy-saving scheme, which rewards reduced peak-time use with a free weekend hour; on Sundays they run the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine, and may charge their electric cars.

Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next (rates below the quarterly Ofgem cap), expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year—up £400 on last year. She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets, and pays by direct debit. She also keeps curtains shut to retain heat, has her daughters wear thermal clothing when cold, and uses less hot water.

Around 1.5 million UK households rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, with costs already rising over the past year due to global oil market disruption. Bradley Knowles, 32, a finance worker in rural Lincolnshire living with his husband, mother and sister, noted that when he moved two years ago a litre of heating oil cost 50-60p; at the height of the Iran war it reached £1.20 or £1.30, now stabilising around £1. He orders oil in bulk—1,000 to 1,500 litres (the candidate readings list "500" as an alternative figure)—preferably in summer when prices are lower and a few weeks ahead to avoid costly next-day delivery.

Bradley uses comparison sites for the cheapest local suppliers, sets aside money monthly so he can always afford orders, and avoids leaving oil-powered boilers on all day. Instead he uses an electric tank to store warm water and tops up heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.
items.title: BBC Profiles Three UK Households Cutting Energy Costs Amid January Price-Cap Rise

items.summary: The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission filed two lawsuits against Alphabet's Google on Wednesday (Nov 25), seeking a combined RM600 million (US$146 million) in damages, alleging the company failed to take adequate action against harmful content. The regulator said Google had not adequately addressed online gambling, scams and fraud on its YouTube platform or taken proactive measures regarding "various volatile contents" associated with a well-known blogger. According to Malaysian news outlet The Star, that blogger is Wan Muhammad Azri, better known as Papagomo, who was charged in 2024 for seditious remarks linking the Malaysian government to being pro-Israel and pro-West on Facebook. In its statement about the two lawsuits, the regulator said the damages sought were intended to remedy the substantial resources and manpower expended in addressing more than 50,000 harmful online contents arising from Google's systemic failure and to ensure a safe social media platform. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The suits come just weeks after Google announced it would invest US$15 billion in Malaysia from 2027 to 2028 toward data centre campuses, clean energy, water security and worker upskilling. Malaysia's government has maintained a testy relationship with major social media firms including TikTok and previously Meta Platforms' Facebook, accusing them of failing to remove content it deems harmful.
items.title: Malaysian Regulator Sues Google for $146 Million Over Harmful Content

items.summary: The text describes how China engages with partner countries through its Belt and Road Initiative, highlighting two specific collaborations. Greece was the first EU member state to sign a Belt and Road cooperation document with China; according to the source, this collaboration has helped breathe new life into the Port of Piraeus, which serves as a vital gateway connecting Greece to the wider world. Similarly, Senegal was the first country in West Africa to sign such an agreement with China, and their partnership is described as continuing to grow while opening what the source calls "new chapters of shared opportunity" for both nations. The text frames these relationships within a broader narrative about two ancient civilizations sharing bonds spanning more than two millennia.
items.title: China's Belt and Road Partnerships Revive Piraeus Port and Expand in West Africa

items.summary: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) approved on Wednesday the takeover of 14 private hospitals by not-for-profit Catholic healthcare operator Calvary from collapsed provider Healthscope. The acquisition is still dependent on state governments issuing hospital licences, with a date not yet confirmed. Under the proposed deal, reproductive services including IVF, elective abortions, voluntary assisted dying (VAD) and gender reassignment procedures would cease at any hospitals currently offering them. The 14 hospitals include six in New South Wales, four in Victoria, two in Brisbane, and one each in the Northern Territory and South Australia; they comprise private hospitals as well as rehabilitation clinics. Calvary welcomed the decision in a statement on Wednesday. The ACCC’s assessment examined only competition impacts, finding “no real likelihood of any operator other than Calvary buying the 14 hospitals”, which were unlikely to remain open otherwise, while acknowledging concerns raised by medical practitioners and community members that some services would no longer be provided if the acquisition proceeded. Ahead of the announcement, New South Wales health minister Ryan Park said the state government would support access to IVF at John Hunter and Newcastle private hospital through theatre access at publicly run John Hunter hospital, adding that “the vast majority of [other] services will either continue or be available through alternative local providers”. The ACCC has already approved Calvary’s acquisition of Hobart private hospital, with the provider assuming responsibility next month, and took over Holmesglen private hospital in Melbourne last month. As a Catholic healthcare provider, Calvary says it is guided by Catholic Health Australia’s code of ethics, which states any action or omission that “causes death with the purpose of eliminating all suffering” is not permissible; the provider said it will work with clinicians to provide pathways for treatments no longer offered under the acquisition. Dr Linda Swan, CEO of charity Go Gentle Australia, called the ACCC decision “disappointing but not unexpected”, saying she was “deeply concerned that Calvary’s acquisitions will reduce choice for dying people” and warned that relocating seriously unwell end-of-life patients is difficult and can cause distress and trauma while increasing pressure on bed-short public hospitals. NSW Greens health spokesperson Amanda Cohn said the state government had added “insult to injury” by allowing Calvary to continue operating the troubled public-private partnership at Calvary Mater hospital in Newcastle, where cancer or end-of-life care patients have already been transferred to Newcastle private for VAD access; she asked where these patients would go now that this option is gone. Dr Nisha Khot, president of Ranzcog, said the acquisition could put “more pressure on the public healthcare system” where Calvary is the only private option, noting women on a public waitlist for gynecological surgery might not get it because IVF patients are prioritised instead. Endocrinologist Prof Ada Cheung, head of the Trans Health Research Group, said state governments need to guarantee all forms of care, warning that gender-affirming surgery is mainly delivered privately at significant cost with very limited public access across Australia, so losing options means people “travel further, pay more and wait longer”.
items.title: ACCC Approves Calvary Takeover of 14 Private Hospitals, Ending IVF, Abortion, VAD and Gender-Affirming Care

items.summary: A Zimbabwean court issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of late former president Robert Mugabe and his second wife Grace Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court on Tuesday. He was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over allegations that they assaulted a police officer using their hands and broomsticks during an investigation into suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles; prosecutors also allege the group took and smashed the officer's phone and seized his loaded pistol. The five men faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property, were granted bail on 6 November, and had been due back in court that day. While Mugabe failed to attend, his co-accused—an aide and three security guards—appeared and were remanded until 10 December; the group has yet to enter pleas. Bellarmine Chatunga is Robert Mugabe's youngest son from Grace Mugabe. Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017 at age 93 following a military intervention, and died in 2019. In recent legal troubles, his son admitted to drug-related charges involving cannabis possession last month; he was deported from South Africa in April after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm while illegally in the country, having been arrested over the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home; and in 2023 he was arrested in Harare over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party before being freed following an out-of-court settlement with the complainant.}
items.title: Zimbabwe Issues Arrest Warrant for Robert Mugabe's Son Over Missed Court Date

The Albanese government secured the Greens' agreement to eliminate fuel tax subsidies for private jet owners, allowing Labor to advance a minimum 30% tax rate on discretionary trust income. The deal was reached as parliament nears its end of year sitting period, with four key pieces of legislation—including a gas reservation scheme—still pending.

Under the arrangement, wealthy private aircraft operators will no longer receive fuel excise subsidies that had let them pay roughly one-fifteenth (below 4 cents per litre) compared to ordinary motorists at 54 cents per litre. Greens leader David Shoebridge described the change as forcing ultra-wealthy individuals like Gina Rinehart, Clive Palmer, and Pauline Hanson to match the effective tax rate paid by regular Australians from 2029-30.

The discretionary trust tax is estimated to raise $4.5bn in its first year of operation. In exchange for Greens support on this measure, Labor agreed to carve out pensioners from reductions to private health insurance rebates for over-65s—a concession following the bill's earlier rejection by the Senate last month.

Shoebridge said the health rebate changes would prevent 1.2 million pensioners from paying more, noting around 2 million insured older Australians lived on less than $37,000 a year. Labor had promised to spend $3bn in savings from the budget measure on additional aged care beds; Health Minister Mark Butler confirmed the government would fund that amount despite the concession.

The Greens also backed digital duty of care legislation Wednesday afternoon after negotiating stronger penalties including "multibillion-dollar" fines and allowing individuals to sue social media companies. Industry Minister Madeleine King told News24 that each senator must decide whether to support Aussie gas for Aussies, with Labor still intending to pass the remaining laws this week.
items.title: Labor Wins Greens Support for Trust Tax Changes in Exchange for Scrapping Jet Fuel Subsidies

items.summary: Japan's debate over defense spending is heading toward a final showdown as a year-end deadline approaches for a five-year plan. Proponents of fiscal sustainability are pushing for a ¥50 trillion to ¥60 trillion budget, while defense hawks argue for at least ¥70 trillion. The ultimate amount could affect progress in Japan's defense buildup and its relationship with the U.S. As part of revisions to three key security documents due by year-end, the Defense Ministry lobbied for an increase to as much as ¥80 trillion over the next five years — nearly doubling the ¥43 trillion plan announced in 2022.
items.title: Fight over Defense Spending in Japan Enters Final Showdown

items.summary:
Senegal regained the Africa Cup of Nations title on Tuesday when the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) overturned a March ruling that had awarded the trophy to Morocco. The dispute traces to January's final in Morocco, which Senegal won 1-0 after extra time following a chaotic match featuring violent clashes in the stands and ball boys involved in scuffles over towels used by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy. At 0-0 with 15 minutes remaining, Senegal walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick; referee Jean-Jacques Ndala of Congo then allowed play to resume after a delay. Morocco's Brahim Diaz converted his penalty with a Panenka chip shot that was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.

In March 2025, CAF-appointed appeal judges reversed the result as a 3-0 default win for Morocco, citing tournament regulations stating a team that leaves the ground before regular time ends without referee authorization is considered to have lost. CAS rejected that ruling on Tuesday, with its three judges unanimous in finding referee Ndala did not err in law and had sole authority to resume play after both teams returned to the pitch.

CAS director general Matthieu Reeb acknowledged receiving a Moroccan protest just minutes before announcing the verdict; his panel conceded there were insufficient grounds at that stage to postpone notification. CAS noted its field-of-play doctrine holds that on-field referee calls generally cannot be challenged, and described Ndala's decision as not arbitrary or affected by external factors.

The legal battle may continue after Morocco announced plans to appeal likely to Switzerland's supreme court in a challenge targeting German arbitrator Ulrich Haas, alleging confirmed communication between Haas and Senegalese federation president Abdoulaye Fall 48 hours before the decision. CAS director Reeb said the panel handling petitions for challenge conceded there were not enough elements at that stage to postpone notification of the award.

Patrick Kabou, a lawyer for the Senegalese Soccer Federation, called the alleged communication between Fall and Haas "unreal." Morocco's federation protested what it described as CAS's failure to address potential integrity concerns. Haas has been among the most respected CAS judges in the past 20 years, selected for cases involving Manchester City's Champions League ban appeal, Simona Halep's doping case, and Africa's Champions League final in 2019.

CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court only on limited procedural grounds including a judge's integrity. CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and promised a verdict by end of November with a full written ruling setting out their reasons.

Senegal paraded with the trophy ahead of its March game against Peru even though Morocco was recognized as champion then; both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves Africa's rightful champions. CAS rulings have stripped athletes of Olympic medals for doping, but overturning a major soccer competition result is rare — the court refused to change results in the 2019 Asian Cup and African Champions League final cases.

The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end its title wait of 50 years. Senegalese fans celebrated; Mariama Sidibé, a 35-year-old accountant in Dakar, said the court confirmed Senegal as Africa's real champions and suggested both countries should focus on what unites them while hoping for Moroccan revenge next summer. Sidi Sylla, a philosophy student at Dakar's main university, called the ruling not just a win for Senegal but for football generally.
items.title: Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco

items.summary:
Four years after NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately collided with the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022, ESA's Hera mission has arrived at the Didymos–Dimorphos binary system to investigate the aftermath of that planetary-defense test. The first images from Hera are set to be released later on Wednesday.

DART targeted Dimorphos, a small moonlet about 150m (490ft) wide orbiting its larger parent asteroid Didymos, roughly 730m (2,400ft) across. The spacecraft struck at approximately 22,000km per hour (14,000mph), and the resulting debris trail measured about 10,000km long (6,200 miles). Before the collision, Dimorphos took 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit Didymos; after DART's impact, that orbital period shortened by roughly 33 minutes, demonstrating that an asteroid's path can be altered.

Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission, described the spacecraft as "a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene." He noted that because DART was destroyed on impact—"Dart exploded in the asteroid"—scientists lack information about its final state. The collision may have left a crater whose size and depth remain unknown, or it could have entirely reshaped Dimorphos.

Hera will spend the next year studying both asteroids, carrying instruments plus two small shoe-box-sized satellites that can examine the impact site up close before landing on the asteroid. A key objective is measuring Dimorphos's mass to determine how effective DART's shove was and what it would take to deflect a future Earth-bound object.

Prof Simon Green of Hera's science team explained this data could help predict deflection requirements: "We [could] measure its properties and say... we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth." Carolyn Ernst of Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory emphasized that medium-sized asteroids—around Dimorphos's dimensions—"could wipe out a city," while larger ones could cause global devastation.

The article also notes plans for future missions: NASA's Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor space telescope is set to launch in 2027, and two spacecraft—including NASA's Osiris-APEX and the ESA-JAXA joint mission Ramses—will visit asteroid Apophis. Apophis, about 450m (1,480ft) long, was initially feared to hit Earth on April 13, 2029, but scientists now believe it will not threaten humanity for at least the next 100 years and instead pass just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above the surface.
items.title: ESA's Hera Spacecraft Arrives to Assess DART Impact on Dimorphos

items.summary: Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said Australia's leadership at COP31 in Türkiye ended without a deal after several countries and the 27-nation European Union rejected a final proposal that did not mention fossil fuels. The rejection occurred on Sunday afternoon, with Australia and Türkiye sharing summit leadership.
items.title: Frustrated Bowen Says Geopolitical Tensions Hurt COP Consensus

King Philippe of Belgium inaugurated Tuesday what is to become the EU's largest satellite factory, located in the southern city of Charleroi and operated by Belgian firm Aerospacelab. The facility aims to meet growing European demand for space infrastructure as part of Europe's push toward greater self-reliance amid concerns about US reliability.

The megafactory has an annual production capacity of roughly 500 satellites, though it is currently idle with staff set to move in during January and production targeted to begin by the end of 2028. The facility spans approximately 20,000 square metres and will produce among other things satellites for the European Union's Iris2 project.

The Iris2 constellation aims to rival Elon Musk's Starlink. In September, Aerospacelab CEO Benoit Deper and his partners secured a €2.4 billion contract to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for the Iris2 constellation. Deper noted that his company has grown from a "tiny startup" in 2018 into a large-scale project contributing to Europe's space sovereignty, stating they have "grown even faster than our own ambitions."
items.title: Belgium Opens Europe's Largest Satellite Factory in Charleroi

items.summary:
Residents of Queensland's Northern Peninsula Area (NPA) are enduring lengthy, rolling water outages as reservoir levels fall to critical lows during a prolonged heatwave. Mains water has been cut across the five communities—New Mapoon, Injinoo, Umagico, Bamaga and Seisia—with short notice since early September, often from 9pm to 6am on allocated days.

The Bureau of Meteorology has issued heatwave warnings for several weeks, with recent forecasts calling for temperatures in the low 40s Celsius and overnight minimums in the mid-20s. Veolia, the council's water contractor, warned in early November that storage levels were critically low after power outages disrupted pumping from the Jardine River.

Northern Peninsula Area Regional Council (NPARC) uses its Facebook page to provide updates, but resident Kawia Akinsola said not everyone receives messages—particularly older people and those with disabilities—who may be unaware water is off until the last minute. She noted many households are overcrowded and stored water runs out quickly.

The region has about 2,800 people living in 1,090 dwellings according to the 2021 Census. NPARC installed an emergency backup generator to recharge reservoirs but is switching off supplies overnight across alternating communities.

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli called the restrictions "completely unacceptable" and said his government invested in water pumps and pipes in New Mapoon and Bamaga as part of the $10 million joint federal-state Northern Peninsula Area Water Supply Project. The project includes upgrades to the Bamaga Water Treatment Plant, increasing capacity to a proposed nine megalitres a day, replacing asbestos-cement water pipes and connecting a new main in New Mapoon.

Federal Water Minister Murray Watt said the investment would support long-term infrastructure improvements. However, Cook MP David Kempton questioned whether the planned works would resolve ongoing supply issues, noting uncertainty about the condition of remaining asbestos pipes.

In March, NPARC's Local Resilience Action Plan identified securing a second pipeline from the Jardine River as a critical priority; that project remains unfunded. The council is also considering a second raw water pond estimated to cost $4 million to increase storage capacity.
items.title: Cape York residents face overnight water outages amid critically low reservoirs during heatwave

items.summary: Several hundred protesters gathered outside the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday to oppose a controversial bill on pesticides. Demonstrators say the proposed legislation could weaken existing safeguards, allowing unlimited authorizations for certain pesticides and extending the periods during which banned products can remain on the market. The crowd included campaigners, farmers, scientists, and cancer victims, who called on MEPs to protect public health and reject the changes. According to the protesters, the bill has raised concerns over the potential impact of pesticide exposure on human health and the environment.
items.title: Protesters Rally Outside European Parliament Against Pesticide Bill

items.summary: Chinese technology companies have increased investment in research and development while accelerating innovation across AI computing power, cloud services, large language models, and commercial applications. Alibaba's financial results show revenue from AI cloud and computing services grew 53% year on year, with external commercialization revenue rising 64%, as AI-related product revenue has recorded triple-digit growth for 13 consecutive quarters. At the Yunqi Conference, Alibaba's chip subsidiary T-Head unveiled its next-generation Zhenwu V900 AI chip, scheduled to go on sale in the first quarter of 2027, alongside a next-generation supernode product powered by the chip. Tencent continues upgrading its Hunyuan large language model with more computing resources allocated to model-as-a-service offerings and GPU leasing; when Hy4 was released in November, it ranked first among Chinese models on the Agent Arena leaderboard for task success rate, user satisfaction, and steerability. WorkBuddy has become China's most widely used AI product by token consumption, with over 10 million users collectively consuming more than 100 trillion tokens daily while its enterprise customer base grows. In Egypt, Chinese companies have covered computing services and training costs for eligible startups to help develop Arabic-language models, lowering barriers to entry for local businesses. The Hill reported that as Chinese AI products gain use across Africa, Asia, and Latin America—supporting infrastructure, classrooms, airports, and government services—localized cloud services are helping expand their presence in the Global South. Tan Poh Hwee, president of the Asia Academy of Digital Economics in Singapore, told Xinhua that China's notable contribution has been moving technologies from laboratories into large-scale production; a model in Singapore's national Sea-Lion series is based on a Chinese AI model so local teams can focus resources on regional languages and industry-specific knowledge. Simon Bridges, CEO of the Auckland Business Chamber in New Zealand, said at the APEC CEO Summit that cooperation remains important amid the current global landscape, citing open-source models as an example of China making technological benefits more accessible across the region.
items.title: Chinese AI Companies Report Strong Growth and Expand Global Reach

items.summary: Bilateral trade between China and Italy exceeded €60 billion in the first nine months of 2026, with Italian exports to China rising by around 20% year on year, according to Italian Ambassador to China Massimo Ambrosetti. The figures were cited at the 13th Notte Italiana gala held in Beijing on November 21, an event organized by the China-Italy Chamber of Commerce (CICC) that brought together roughly 500 guests, including Chinese and Italian institutional representatives and business leaders.
items.title: China-Italy bilateral trade surpasses €60 billion as Italy promotes economic ties at Beijing gala

items.summary: A South African court on Tuesday convicted and sentenced Tafadzwa Sithole, a Zimbabwean man, for attempting to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine. He was arrested earlier this month along with eight others after entering South Africa legally on November 4 and staying at accommodation in Kempton Park, east of Johannesburg, in preparation for his journey. On November 8, he was arrested at O.R. Tambo International Airport while attempting to board a flight to Russia.
items.title: South African Court Convicts Zimbabwean Man of Attempting to Join Russian War

items.summary: The Saudi-led coalition announced Wednesday that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura in the kingdom's Eastern Province, according to a statement posted on X by coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki. Maliki said several fragments fell during the operation and an initial assessment found no injuries. The interceptions followed a drone attack one day earlier that targeted a tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District, injuring 11 people per Saudi Civil Defense; Maliki blamed Yemen's Houthi group for both incidents amid escalating hostilities between the Houthis and coalition forces.
items.title: Saudi-led Coalition Intercepts Drones Over Eastern Province as Regional Tensions Escalate

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has reinstated Senegal as the winner of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, overturning an earlier decision that had awarded the trophy to Morocco after Senegalese players walked off the pitch during the final. The ruling came after returning to the field, Senegal won the match 1-0 in extra time; a prior appeals panel had instead ruled a 3-0 default victory for Morocco.

Morocco's Football Federation has vowed to pursue "all necessary legal avenues" and said it could take the case to Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court. The federation objected to what it called "contact" between one of the CAS panel members and the head of the Senegalese football federation days before the decision was announced.

Moroccan fans reacted with disappointment, though responses varied. Jad Ouchtaqalla said he had hoped the tournament would stay in Morocco because his country deserved it and expressed shock at the decision. Amine Saadi accepted the outcome but noted they would have liked to keep the trophy there and hope to win a future edition. Fan Rachid Debbi, by contrast, was not surprised by the ruling, saying he had expected Senegal to be awarded the trophy since they initially took it.

items.title: Morocco to challenge CAS ruling reinstating Senegal as AFCON champions

The Reserve Bank of India has proposed the Draft Amendment Directions for 'Preventive Safeguards for Electronic Banking Transactions (EBTs),' which would come into force on July 1, 2027, or earlier at a bank's discretion. Some provisions expanding the definition of bank negligence are set to take effect from January 1, 2027.

Under the proposed rules, customers can switch off digital payment facilities, set transaction limits and temporarily block all outgoing payments through a stop switch facility that immediately disables outward future debits linked to their account. However, this would not cover recurring payment mandates or standing instructions, liens for due charges or loan instalments, bank-initiated recovery debits, inward credits into the account, new UPI registrations on third-party apps, or creation of new payment mandates and standing instructions.

The RBI has also proposed a Trusted Person Mechanism (TPM) as an additional authentication layer. Customers could register a trusted person aged 18 years or above to authenticate certain electronic fund transfers through physical and digital banking channels when the transaction exceeds a customer-set threshold, but not for UPI-linked payments, merchant payments or recurring standing instructions.

Customers may gain greater control over debit card, credit card and prepaid payment instrument transactions by switching on or off different types of transactions and setting or modifying limits within overall issuer-prescribed limits. Banks would also have to provide facilities to set or modify transaction limits for digital payment channels other than cards.

The RBI proposes that banks keep all digital payment channels disabled by default at customer onboarding, enabling them only upon explicit consent with applicable authentication requirements. For debit and credit cards issued by the RBI, physical and virtual cards should be enabled initially only for contact-based usage (ATMs and Point of Sale devices) within India, while forex prepaid cards would be enabled for both contact and contactless use outside India.

For other digital payment channels, banks enabling a channel at onboarding or later must specify an aggregate ceiling on fund transfers over the initial 24 hours, with gradual enhancements allowed afterward based on channel risk assessment and internal policy. The draft also defines bank negligence as any act of omission or commission contributing to fraudulent electronic banking transactions, including failures in authentication instructions, multi-factor authentication for new account linkages, mandatory alerts, fraud reporting channels, prompt action on customer notifications, blocking digital payment channels after failed login attempts, providing customer-induced controls and the Trusted Person Mechanism, system malfunctions or security breaches, and employee collusion.
items.title: RBI Proposes Stricter Rules Against Digital Fraud

E-commerce company Amazon announced Wednesday that it has reached $27 billion in cumulative exports from India through its Amazon Global Selling programme, with the number of exporters on the platform rising 20 per cent over a year to 2.4 lakh (approximately 240,000). The milestone marks progress toward Amazon's goal of enabling $80 billion in cumulative e-commerce exports from India by 2030, according to a company statement.

The programme was launched in 2015 and has enabled the sale of more than one billion 'Made-in-India' products to customers across Amazon's global marketplaces. Among states and Union Territories, Delhi topped the list with over 36,000 exporters, followed by Rajasthan (over 32,500), Uttar Pradesh (over 29,000), Gujarat (over 28,000) and Maharashtra (over 23,500).

Among smaller cities, exporters from Erode in Tamil Nadu crossed $121.5 million in sales between January 2025 and the third quarter of 2026.

Health and personal care (45 per cent), groceries (44 per cent), beauty (42 per cent) and toys (35 per cent) emerged as the top-performing categories, recording the highest compound annual growth rates over the last 10 years.
items.title: Amazon's e-commerce exports from India reach $27 billion as exporter count rises 20%

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has identified a growing gap between installed solar power capacity and Chinese panel imports across developing countries in Africa, West Asia, and Southeast Asia, which it terms the "missing PV panels" phenomenon. The IEA attributes this discrepancy to increasing reliance on decentralized off-grid solar systems among consumers with limited electricity access or facing daily blackouts of 8-10 hours, noting that such grid-unconnected installations are difficult for governments to track and thus classified as off-grid in its dataset.

The West Asia conflict, which erupted on February 20, 2026, served as a tailwind for the trend. The IEA reported that amid energy market disruptions from the conflict, solar panel imports from China into Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia rose sharply during March to May of this year.

The gap is most pronounced in Pakistan, where official statistics report only around 10 GW of installed solar PV capacity as of March 2026, but imports reached nearly 50 GW from 2020 to 2025. The IEA noted that although Pakistan shows the largest absolute gap compared with Africa and ASEAN, many developing economies with limited electricity access register a discrepancy of over 50 per cent.

The trend is projected to drive significant off-grid solar PV expansion in the IEA's forecast: growth for 2026-2031 is expected to increase 2.5-fold from the 2020-2025 period, with almost 80 GW of off-grid capacity to be installed through 2031. Outside Pakistan, Sub-Saharan Africa is set to lead this surge with more than 21 GW of new installations over 2026-2031—equivalent to the region's total installed capacity today. In ASEAN, about 10 GW of additional off-grid capacity is projected—a tenfold increase from a current capacity of less than 1 GW.

The IEA also noted that these "missing" panels reflect global trade complexities, as some Chinese-imported solar PV panels are re-exported to developing economies to avoid tariffs in other markets.
items.title: IEA Points to Hidden Solar Boom in Developing Regions via 'Missing PV Panels'

items.summary: Amazon has launched a platform for buying and selling new and used cars online in the United Kingdom, positioning itself as a key player in UK car sales. Hyundai will be among the first automakers to partner with the service, offering both new and used electric, hybrid, and petrol vehicles including the IONIQ 3, IONIQ 5, KONA, and i20 models. Used cars from dealer group Vertu Motors will also be available when the platform launches. Amazon stated it plans to bring additional brands and dealerships on board in coming months.

New records reviewed by Reuters shed light on the business network around Alice Huang, whose family and associates financed hundreds of millions of dollars in AI computing equipment in China. The financing documents filed in a Chinese central-bank credit registry identify up to 764 AI servers and computing modules along with $31 million in networking equipment used to connect large computing systems. Much of the hardware was listed at a sprawling Shanghai data centre developed by gaming company Century Huatong, in which Tencent holds roughly a 10% minority stake.

The financing arrangements offer a fresh look at how businesses connected to Huang's family and associates helped build and fund China's AI computing infrastructure, even as US authorities investigate whether her Singapore-based company Megaspeed helped Chinese customers obtain restricted Nvidia technology. The network has also drawn scrutiny over its links to China's defence sector and the People's Liberation Army (PLA). Corporate records and research by intelligence firm Strider Technologies reviewed by The New York Times have connected companies associated with Huang's family and business partners to Chinese state-owned defence contractors and military-linked businesses.

The connections do not establish that the servers identified in the latest Reuters report were used by the PLA or contained chips prohibited from export to China. One of the key businesses involved was Century Litong, an Nvidia preferred cloud partner that rents powerful servers to customers requiring large amounts of computing capacity. Financial records show five leasing arrangements covering up to 512 servers with a declared value of 1.42 billion yuan, or about $200 million, between May and December 2024.

Four of the arrangements listed equipment at the Yangtze River Delta AI supercomputing centre in Shanghai, a complex developed by Century Huatong where Tencent holds roughly 10%. A separate transaction involved 128 servers worth $57 million financed by an arm of the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC), a state-backed aviation and defence conglomerate, and leased to Century Litong. Another inventory listed more than 10,000 Nvidia ConnectX-7 networking cards and 730 BlueField-3 units at the Shanghai facility.

In April 2026, Wuhu Century Longteng, a company majority-owned by Huang's sister Huang Yu through investment vehicles until early 2026, pledged another 252 AI computing modules as collateral for a $70 million loan from Ping An Bank. The dollar values reflect assets covered by financing arrangements and do not necessarily represent new spending or separate purchases.

The latest records add to questions about the business network surrounding Alice Huang, her sister Huang Yu and Kang Wei, her business partner who is often described as her husband. Corporate records connect Century Litong, Century Longteng and Century Huatong to Huang Yu and Kang. Lettall also owns Nanjing Jinning Microwave, a manufacturer of components used in Chinese radar and missile systems according to company disclosures cited by The New York Times.

The network also has links to AVIC through financing arrangements involving its affiliate. Other corporate connections identified by Strider include China Electronics Technology Group, a military-electronics conglomerate. A Strider analysis reviewed by The New York Times found that about $3.6 billion in Chinese government money had flowed through companies associated with Huang's family and business associates.

"Follow the money and, too often, you find the PLA at the end of it," Strider chief executive Greg Levesque told the newspaper. The links are often indirect; the research does not establish that the PLA used computing power from data centres connected to Huang's family.

Tencent's minority stake in Century Huatong has brought another prominent Chinese technology company into scrutiny surrounding the network. The US Department of Defense included Tencent on its list of Chinese military companies operating in the United States under Section 1260H, a designation identifying companies the Pentagon considers linked to China's military that does not itself impose an immediate ban.

Tencent has disputed the designation, saying it was a mistake and that the company was not a military supplier. The company also told Reuters that it had never owned or operated the Yangtze River Delta Data Center Cluster Project and that its name and trademarks had previously been used without authorisation. Tencent said its investment in Century Huatong was related to the gaming business and that it had no commercial relationship with Megaspeed.

The records reviewed by Reuters do not establish that Tencent bought, rented or operated the specific servers identified in the financing documents. Alice Huang formerly controlled Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company and major overseas buyer of Nvidia processors. The US Commerce Department added the company to its trade blacklist on Monday.

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and said Huang left the company in August 2025. Separately, US intelligence agencies have reportedly gathered information about Huang's contacts with China's Ministry of State Security (MSS), including during part of her relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The agencies are also said to have gathered evidence suggesting Kang Wei worked with the same intelligence agency according to reports citing people familiar with the intelligence.

The extent of the alleged intelligence work remains under investigation. China has denied allegations that Alice Huang was a spy. The latest financing records do not establish that the servers contained export-restricted chips or show how and when the equipment entered China, but they reveal the scale of the computing infrastructure financed by companies connected to Huang's family and associates in a network which also finds its ties to the Chinese military.
items.title: Nvidia Chip Scandal: Alice Huang's $270 Million Network Linked to China's Military

items.summary: A Delhi District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (South II) directed Amazon Seller Services Pvt Ltd to pay Rs 20,000 compensation to a customer who received two packets of rakhis instead of four silver coins worth Rs 5,996. The order was passed on November 13 and held the e-commerce platform guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practices under Section 6(1) of the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules.
items.title: Delhi Consumer Commission Orders Amazon to Pay Rs 20,000 After Customer Received Rakhis Instead of Silver Coins
